title: How To Praise With Power
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin opens with a scene of a teacher quietly praising a struggling student at recess, using it to illustrate what makes praise genuinely effective. He identifies four qualities behind the teacher's impact: the praise was based in truth and tied to real accomplishment, it was reserved so that the student valued earning it, it was delivered privately rather than in front of the class, and it came from authentic emotion rather than a scripted response. He warns that false praise or 'caught being good' manipulation lowers a classroom's bar of excellence and dilutes the currency of recognition. Linsin also challenges the common advice that praise must be immediate, arguing a delayed private moment can carry more weight. The article closes by urging teachers to reserve a simple 'thank you' for routine compliance and save real, heartfelt praise for performance that is genuinely noteworthy.
points: Effective praise must be based on truth and tied to real achievement, not given to placate or manipulate.
Reserving praise for genuine accomplishment makes it something students actively seek and value.
Private praise, delivered one-on-one, has more lasting impact than public praise given in front of the class.
Praise doesn't have to be immediate—waiting to deliver it privately can increase its power.
Use a simple 'thank you' for routine, expected performance and save genuine praise for truly noteworthy accomplishment.
quotes: Her words had power because she praised him in a way that mattered to him, in a way that sparked his intrinsic motivational engine. And this makes all the difference.

Any and all praise you offer your students must be based on truth. It must be in response to real accomplishment rather than a self-interested desire to placate , flatter, or manipulate the student into behaving.
She steadfastly refused to lower the bar of excellence in her classroom by engaging in false praise and “caught being good” manipulation.
The more impressive the accomplishment, the more important it is to pull the student aside to offer your praise.
And contrary to the oft-repeated advice that praise must always be immediate, giving your students a moment or more to enjoy their successes before jumping in can be much more powerful.
If a student performs a routine, direction, task, or procedure as taught, then a simple ‘thank you’ will do.
If, however, you witness performance that is truly noteworthy, then speak from the heart. Make your praise genuine.
